title: Cynergy Bank Savings Accounts: Rates, Bonus Trap and Verdict
meta_title: Cynergy Bank: 5.05% One-Year Bond, Easy Access Now Closed
meta_description: Cynergy has closed its easy access account to new savers. What is left: a 5.05% one-year bond, notice to 4.18%, and a loyalty rate most never see.
intro:
Cynergy Bank’s one-year Fixed Rate Bond pays 5.05% AER, read from Cynergy’s own rates page on 7 October 2026, and it is now the only competitive thing the bank sells to a new customer. The Online Easy Access Account — the bonus-inflated headline that put Cynergy on every best-buy table — now carries the line “available for our existing customers only”. If you do not already hold one, you cannot open one.

That one-year rate beats every other term Cynergy offers, including the five-year at 4.30%. The curve is not merely flat, it is inverted, and sharply: locking money away for five times as long pays you 75 basis points less.

There is a second structure to understand before comparing Cynergy with anyone else. Every bond and fixed cash ISA is published at two rates: an advertised rate for new money and a loyalty rate, up to 0.85 percentage points higher, available only when a maturing Cynergy account funds it. On the two and three-year bonds the gap is 80 and 85 basis points — 4.20% advertised against 5.00% and 5.05% loyalty. Any single-figure quote for a Cynergy bond is therefore telling you only half the story, and quite possibly the wrong half.

sections.heading: The easy access account, and why it still matters
sections.html:
Cynergy’s easy access pricing is now a closed book, but it is worth reading if you are already in it. The account pays 4.15% AER with a bonus for the first twelve months and 2.15% AER without it. Both figures are Cynergy’s own: the bank used to publish only the headline, leaving the underlying rate to be worked out by subtraction, and it now prints both side by side. That is a straightforward improvement in disclosure and it confirms the two-point gap.

So an existing customer who opened the account on its old 4.55% headline should treat month eleven as a deadline. Once the bonus falls away the money is sitting at 2.15%, which is behind Close Brothers’ unconditional 3.85% and barely ahead of Aldermore’s 2.25%. Because the account is closed to new customers, you also cannot reset the clock by opening a fresh one — the usual bonus-hopping move is off the table here.

  • Status: closed to new customers
  • With bonus: 4.15% AER, first 12 months
  • Without bonus: 2.15% AER, published by Cynergy
  • Withdrawals: unlimited and free, no notice, no rate penalty

The Online ISA at 4.15% AER variable is still open, takes £1 and accepts transfers in. It now pays exactly what the easy access account pays with its bonus attached, tax-free rather than taxable, which makes it the more sensible home for anyone near their personal savings allowance.

sections.heading: An inverted bond ladder, and two rates for every rung
sections.html:
Minimum £1,000, maximum £1,000,000, with a 14-day funding window and no withdrawals once the term is underway. Interest is paid into the bond and cannot be paid away, which rules the product out for anyone drawing an income from their capital.

The rates, advertised first and loyalty second:

  • 6 months — 4.57% / 4.58%
  • 1 year — 5.05% / 5.06%
  • 15 months — 4.40% / 4.65%
  • 18 months — 4.40% / 4.65%
  • 2 years — 4.20% / 5.00%
  • 3 years — 4.20% / 5.05%
  • 4 years — 4.25% / 4.26%
  • 5 years — 4.30% / 4.35%

Read the advertised column on its own and the conclusion is blunt: take the one year at 5.05% and nothing else. The 15 and 18-month bonds pay 65 basis points less than the one-year for holding your money longer, and the two and three-year pay 85 less. There is no term at which a new saver is rewarded for committing beyond twelve months.

The loyalty column changes the shape completely — 5.00% at two years and 5.05% at three make the ladder behave normally — but those rates need a maturing Cynergy account to fund them, so they are a reason to stay rather than a reason to arrive. Judge the bank on the advertised column, then treat loyalty as what it is: a retention offer you may qualify for in a year.

Cash ISAs

The one-year Fixed Rate Cash ISA is 4.05% AER advertised and 4.75% loyalty, with a £500 minimum and the £20,000 subscription cap. The 70-point gap is the widest in the range. Closing early costs 180 days’ loss of interest, and it is not a flexible ISA — money taken out cannot be replaced without using fresh allowance.

Notice accounts

Three terms, all with a £500 minimum: 35 day at 4.12%, 95 day at 4.15% and 120 day at 4.18% AER. These were the weakest part of this page when it was last written, quoted from a third-party table and flagged as indicative. They are now read from Cynergy’s own rates page, and the 120-day account at 4.18% is the best rate Cynergy will pay you without locking the money away at all.

sections.heading: Awards, complaint volumes and the loyalty catch
sections.html:
Cynergy carries better independent recognition than its size suggests. The Defaqto Banking Award 2026 for Instant Access Cash ISAs is a consistency measure rather than a snapshot: a product has to sit in the top fifteen for ten of twelve months to qualify, and only 29 products out of 2,114 assessed made the cut across all categories. It is also a Which? Recommended Provider.

On complaints, the Financial Ombudsman Service recorded 83 new cases against Cynergy for the period 1 July 2025 to 31 March 2026 — the second-lowest volume of the five providers in this cluster. Per-firm uphold percentages are published only inside an FOS spreadsheet we could not access, so the proportion of those cases decided in the customer’s favour is unverified.

The loyalty structure deserves one more line, because it has grown since this page was first written. It is no longer a footnote about maturing bonds: it is a second published rate on every bond and every fixed ISA, and on the two and three-year bonds it is worth more than the entire gap between Cynergy and the best rate in this comparison. New money is, by design, offered the worse of the two.

sections.heading: Living with a branchless bank
sections.html:
Cynergy is an online operation: accounts are opened and run through the website or app, and the terms say plainly that the accounts are “not suitable for savers who are unable to use Online Banking”. Deposits and withdrawals move through a nominated UK current account. Reported friction points cluster around slow telephone support at peak times and app-based authentication that some customers find fiddly.

Eligibility is straightforward — you must be 18 or over and UK resident for tax purposes. Existing customers get a Fast Track Apply route inside online banking, which removes most of the re-keying when opening a second or third account, and is also how the loyalty rates are reached.

Deposits are protected by the FSCS up to £120,000 per eligible depositor, and Cynergy states that each holder of a joint account is entitled to compensation up to that limit. One correction to what this page said before: Cynergy does not publish a “£240,000 joint” figure, nor an explicit statement that its licence is unshared, so neither is asserted here. If you hold money with more than one brand, check the licence yourself on the FSCS register before assuming the limits stack.

pros: One-year Fixed Rate Bond at 5.05% AER, the best single rate in this comparison at that term
Notice accounts now verifiable from Cynergy’s own rates page — 35 day 4.12%, 95 day 4.15%, 120 day 4.18% AER
Online ISA at 4.15% AER variable, opens with £1 and accepts transfers in
Cynergy now publishes the underlying easy access rate (2.15%) rather than leaving it to be derived
Defaqto Banking Award 2026 winner for Instant Access Cash ISAs, a 12-month consistency measure
Which? Recommended Provider
Only 83 new FOS cases between July 2025 and March 2026
cons: The Online Easy Access Account is closed to new customers — the rate this bank was known for is not available
The advertised bond ladder is inverted: 5.05% at one year against 4.20% at two and three, and 4.30% at five
Loyalty rates up to 0.85 points higher go only to maturing customers, so new money is offered the worse rate by design
Existing easy access customers drop to 2.15% once the 12-month bonus ends, below Close Brothers’ unconditional 3.85%
Fixed rate bonds pay interest into the bond only — no option to have it paid away, so unsuitable for income
Fixed cash ISA is not flexible, and early closure costs 180 days’ interest
The 1-year fixed cash ISA is only 4.05% advertised, against 4.75% for a loyalty customer
No branches; support is online and telephone only, with reported delays at peak
verdict: Cynergy is a different proposition than it was two months ago, and a narrower one. The easy access account that made its name is closed to new customers, so what is on offer to a new saver is a bond ladder whose only competitive rung is the one-year at 5.05% AER. Take that rung and the bank is worth the £1,000; look past it and the 15-month, 18-month, two and three-year bonds all pay less for a longer commitment, which is not a trade anyone should accept. The 120-day notice account at 4.18% is a quietly decent place for money you can plan four months ahead for, and the Online ISA at 4.15% is reasonable if your savings interest is near your personal savings allowance. It remains the wrong bank for income savers, since bond interest cannot be paid away, and for anyone who wants a branch. Existing easy access customers have one job: find out when the bonus ends, because 2.15% afterwards is beaten by Close Brothers paying 3.85% with no conditions at all.

faqs.q: Can I still open a Cynergy easy access account?
faqs.a: No. Cynergy's Online Easy Access Account states that it is available for existing customers only. If you want easy access with Cynergy you are limited to the Online ISA at 4.15% AER, or a notice account at up to 4.18%.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Cynergy’s advertised and loyalty rates?
faqs.a: Advertised rates are for new money; loyalty rates need a maturing Cynergy account to fund them. The gap is up to 0.85 percentage points — the two-year bond is 4.20% advertised against 5.00% loyalty, and the three-year 4.20% against 5.05%. Quote the advertised rate when comparing Cynergy with another bank, because that is the one you can actually get on day one.

faqs.q: Why does Cynergy pay less for a longer bond?
faqs.a: On the advertised rates it does, and there is no good reason for a saver to accept it. The one-year bond pays 5.05% AER while the five-year pays 4.30% and the two and three-year 4.20%. An inverted curve like that usually means the bank wants short-dated money and is not competing for long. Take the one year, or go elsewhere for the longer term.

faqs.q: Can Cynergy pay my bond interest into my current account?
faqs.a: No. Interest on fixed rate bonds is paid annually into the bond itself and cannot be paid away. Savers who need a regular income from their capital should look at providers that pay interest away — Close Brothers pays annually and at maturity to a nominated account.

faqs.q: Is Cynergy Bank a UK bank and is my money protected?
faqs.a: Yes. Cynergy was Bank of Cyprus UK until it was rebranded in 2018 following a change of ownership, and it is a UK-authorised bank. Eligible deposits are covered by the FSCS up to £120,000 per eligible depositor, with each holder of a joint account entitled to that limit. Cynergy does not publish a statement that its licence is unshared, so check the FSCS register if you hold money with more than one brand.

title: Santander Savings Accounts: What the 8% Actually Pays
meta_description: Santander advertises 8.00% AER — capped at £200 a month. We work out the real returns, the £3 Edge fee, and the 12th-of-17 service ranking.
intro:
No provider in this comparison advertises a bigger number than Santander's 8.00% AER Regular Saver. Very few pay less on money you can actually reach: the standard Easy Access Saver sits at 2.00% AER, and even that rate is only guaranteed for twelve months. That gap between the marketing number and the working number is the whole story of savings at Santander.

Both of the headline products are capped and conditional. The 8.00% takes £200 a month maximum and requires a Santander current account. The 6.00% Edge Saver runs on balances up to £4,000 and is exclusive to holders of the Edge or Explorer current account — and the Edge account charges £3 a month with a £500 monthly funding requirement and two active Direct Debits. Santander is the only provider in this set whose best savings rates sit behind a fee.

Against that, it offers the widest deposit range here — £1 minimum to £2,000,000 maximum on the variable accounts, though the fixed products need £500 — a full branch network that ranks fifth of seventeen for branch service, and an Inheritance ISA that none of its rivals in this cluster match.

sections.heading: The 8% Regular Saver in pounds, not percentages
sections.html:
The Regular Saver pays 8.00% AER variable, of which 5.00 percentage points is a bonus lasting twelve months. You can pay in up to £200 a month, funded from a Santander current account, and Which? currently names it the best-buy regular saver on the market.

The arithmetic matters more than the rate. A regular saver only pays its rate on the balance you have built up so far, so your first £200 earns for twelve months and your last £200 earns for one. Fill it to the maximum every month and you finish the year with £2,400 of your own money and roughly £100 of interest — a real, useful return on a small commitment, but nothing like 8% of £2,400. Treat it as a good place for spare monthly income, not as somewhere to park a lump sum.

When the twelve months are up, the 5.00% bonus disappears and the account reverts to its variable core rate, so the maturity date needs a diary entry.

sections.heading: Edge Saver: 6% behind a £3 monthly fee
sections.html:
The Santander Edge Saver pays 6.00% AER, including a 2.50% bonus for twelve months, on balances up to £4,000. Anything above £4,000 does not earn that rate. Access requires an Edge or Explorer current account; the Edge account costs £3 a month and requires at least £500 paid in monthly plus two active Direct Debits.

Run the numbers before you switch. A full £4,000 at 6.00% generates a maximum of £240 gross interest over a year. The Edge current account fee takes £36 of that, leaving around £204 before any tax — and the fee is payable whether or not the saver is full. The current account has its own separate benefits that may justify the £3 on their own, but if the savings rate is your only reason for holding it, the margin is thinner than 6.00% suggests.

The eligibility conditions are also ongoing, not one-off. Miss the £500 monthly funding or let a Direct Debit lapse and you risk losing the current account benefits that gate the savings rate.

sections.heading: What Santander pays on money you can reach
sections.html:
Away from the two flagship products, the rates are modest:

  • Easy Access Saver: 2.00% AER for 12 months, £1 minimum to £2m
  • Select Easy Access Saver: 2.50% — requires £5,000 a month in deposits or £75,000 in holdings
  • Limited Access Saver: 3.00%, dropping to 1.00% from the third withdrawal in a calendar month
  • Fixed Term Saver: 4.45% at one year, 4.70% at two and three, £500 minimum to £2m, no withdrawals permitted
  • First Home Saver: 4.00% over a 24-month term for first-time buyers, falling to 1.00% if you make more than two withdrawals in a month

For open-access money the 2.00% Easy Access Saver is beaten decisively by Close Brothers at 3.85% with no bonus and no withdrawal limit, and by Cynergy’s 4.15% — though Cynergy has now closed that account to new customers. The Limited Access Saver at 3.00% is competitive only if you genuinely make two or fewer withdrawals a month, every month — the third one costs you two thirds of the rate for that period.

sections.heading: ISAs, including one product nobody else here offers
sections.html:
Santander's tax-free range runs from Fixed Rate ISAs at 4.65% over one year, 4.80% over two, 4.85% over three and 4.90% over five down to an Easy Access ISA at 2.00%, with a Junior ISA at 2.70%. That five-year rate is now the highest fixed ISA figure on the high street side of this comparison, ahead of Nationwide's 4.70%, though both Aldermore (5.03% over three years) and Close Brothers (5.12% over five) pay more. The easy access ISA is not competitive. Note the 30 November 2026 deadline for funding a fixed ISA at these rates, and the 120 days' interest charge for closing one early.

The outlier is the Inheritance ISA at 2.45%, designed for surviving spouses and civil partners of a deceased ISA holder to use their additional permitted subscription. None of Cynergy, Nationwide, Aldermore or Close Brothers offers an equivalent. The rate is unexceptional, but for someone administering an estate the availability of the wrapper at a big high-street bank with branch support may matter more than 50 basis points.

One licence point to check before consolidating: Santander shares its FSCS licence with cahoot. Money held across both brands is covered to a combined £120,000, not £120,000 each.

sections.heading: Branches strong, digital weak: the service picture
sections.html:
The independent CMA/Ipsos service quality survey published in February 2026 places Santander (Great Britain) 12th of 17 for overall service quality at 57% and 12th of 17 for online and mobile banking at 69%. Its branch service is the bright spot: 5th of 17 at 66%. That is a coherent picture — a bank that still does counters well and digital less well.

Complaint volumes reinforce the point. The Financial Ombudsman Service logged 5,261 new cases against Santander UK between 1 July 2025 and 31 March 2026, by far the highest of the five providers here, though Santander also has by far the largest customer base of the group. Uphold percentages are published only in an FOS spreadsheet we could not access and remain unverified.

Santander is not a Which? Recommended Provider and does not appear on the Defaqto Banking Award 2026 recipient list. Cynergy and Aldermore hold both distinctions.

pros: 8.00% AER Regular Saver is the highest headline rate across the providers compared here, and a Which? best buy
£1 minimum and £2,000,000 maximum on the variable accounts — the widest deposit range in this set
Full branch network, ranked 5th of 17 in Great Britain for branch service (66%) in the CMA/Ipsos survey published February 2026
Fixed Rate ISAs from 4.65% to 4.90%, with the five-year the best of the high-street rates here
Inheritance ISA at 2.45% covers a niche no rival in this cluster serves
First Home Saver at 4.00% over 24 months for first-time buyers
cons: The 8.00% is capped at £200 a month and the 6.00% at £4,000 — real returns are far below the headline
Both flagship rates are bonus-inflated (5.00pp and 2.50pp) and both bonuses expire after 12 months
The 6.00% Edge Saver requires a £3-a-month current account with £500 monthly funding and two Direct Debits
Easy Access Saver at 2.00% is well behind Close Brothers (3.85%) on an unconditional rate
Limited Access Saver falls from 3.00% to 1.00% from the third withdrawal in a calendar month
FSCS licence is shared with cahoot — a combined £120,000, not £120,000 per brand
12th of 17 for overall service quality (57%) and for online/mobile banking (69%)
5,261 new FOS cases between July 2025 and March 2026; not a Which? Recommended Provider and absent from the Defaqto Banking Award 2026 list
verdict: Santander works best for someone who already banks there — particularly an Edge or Explorer current account holder who can fill both the £200-a-month Regular Saver and the £4,000 Edge Saver and treat the £3 fee as a cost of the current account rather than the savings. Add a branch requirement and the case strengthens further, since branch service is the one area where Santander measurably outperforms. It is a poor choice for a saver with a larger lump sum and no interest in current account gymnastics: at 2.00% on easy access money, with a licence shared with cahoot and the weakest independently measured digital service in this group, the money is better placed at Close Brothers or Aldermore depending on how long you can lock it away.

faqs.q: How much will I actually earn at 8.00% on the Regular Saver?
faqs.a: Paying in the full £200 every month gives you £2,400 of your own money and roughly £100 of interest over the year. The 8.00% rate applies to the balance you have accumulated at each point, so only the first payment earns for the full twelve months.

faqs.q: Is the £3 Edge current account fee worth paying for the 6.00% saver?
faqs.a: On the savings alone, marginally. A full £4,000 at 6.00% earns up to £240 gross in a year; £36 of fees leaves around £204 before tax, and the fee applies whether or not the saver is full. The Edge account has separate benefits of its own — judge the fee against those as well, not just the savings rate.

faqs.q: Does holding money with cahoot affect my Santander FSCS cover?
faqs.a: Yes. Santander and cahoot share a banking licence, so your balances across both brands are covered to a combined £120,000 per eligible person (£240,000 joint), not £120,000 with each. Split larger sums across separate licences.

faqs.q: Which Santander account is best if I need instant access to a large balance?
faqs.a: Santander's own instant options are weak — 2.00% on the Easy Access Saver, or 2.50% on the Select version if you deposit £5,000 a month or hold £75,000. For unrestricted access at a better rate, Close Brothers pays 3.85% with no bonus and no withdrawal limits, subject to a £10,000 minimum.

faqs.q: Does Santander hold any independent savings awards?
faqs.a: Not in this cycle. It is not a Which? Recommended Provider and does not appear on the Defaqto Banking Award 2026 recipient list. Which? does name its Regular Saver as a current best buy on rate.

title: Nationwide Savings Accounts: Member Rates and the Catch
meta_description: Nationwide refuses to run new-customer bonuses and paid £100 Fairer Share to 4.4m members — but its instant access rate is 1.10–1.20%.
intro:
Nationwide makes a commitment none of its shareholder-owned rivals here will: "Our top savings accounts are only for existing members, and we won't offer 'new customer only' savings accounts." Cynergy's easy access headline contained a 2.00 percentage point bonus, and that account is now closed to new customers altogether; Santander's contain 5.00 and 2.50. Nationwide's contain nothing that expires. That is the cleanest single difference in this comparison.

The price of that stance is that Nationwide's best rates are conditional on membership rather than on being new. The Flex Regular Saver pays 6.50% AER on £200 a month with a Nationwide current account attached; the FlexOne Saver pays 5.00% on up to £5,000 — but only to 11 to 17-year-olds. Walk in off the street with a lump sum and no current account and the society will offer you an Instant Access Saver at 1.10–1.20% tiered, the weakest open-access rate of the five providers reviewed in this cluster.

As the only mutual here, Nationwide also returns money to members directly: £100 each to around 4.4 million members in June 2026, roughly £440m in total and the fourth consecutive year of the Fairer Share Payment.

sections.heading: A pledge no shareholder-owned rival makes
sections.html:
Nationwide's public position is that it will not use new-customer-only savings accounts or teaser bonuses, and will reserve its best pricing for existing members. In practice this reverses the usual trade-off. With Santander, you get the top rate for arriving and a much lower one for staying. With Nationwide, you get very little for arriving and the good rates once you are inside the tent with a current account.

That has a real effect on how you should shop. A loyal saver who dislikes rate-tarting and wants to open an account once has a stronger case for Nationwide than the raw comparison tables suggest, because the rate they see on day one is not scheduled to collapse on day 366. A saver willing to move annually will earn more elsewhere.

Nationwide is a building society, not a bank — the only mutual in this comparison — and is owned by its members rather than shareholders.

sections.heading: The members-only rates, and the 1.05% cliff
sections.html:
Two accounts carry Nationwide's headline pricing, and both come with hard conditions.

Flex Regular Saver — 6.50% AER variable

Maximum £200 a month, requires a Nationwide current account, available from age 16, online only. You get three free withdrawals a year; from the fourth, the rate falls to 1.05%. As with any regular saver, the money-weighted return is well below the headline because the balance builds through the year.

FlexOne Saver — 5.00% AER

Open to 11 to 17-year-olds holding a FlexOne account, on balances up to £5,000. No other provider in this set offers a teenage product at anything approaching that rate — Cynergy, Aldermore and Close Brothers have no under-18 products at all.

Triple Access and Children's saving

The 1 Year Triple Access Saver and ISA pay 3.30% with three free withdrawals, after which the rate drops to 1.05%. The Children's Future Saver pays 2.80% on up to £5,000 a year with two free withdrawals, then 1.35%.

The recurring penalty across the range is that 1.05% floor. Nationwide does not merely reduce your rate when you overstep a withdrawal allowance — it removes most of it.

sections.heading: Fixed bonds and cash ISAs up to 4.70%
sections.html:
Nationwide's fixed pricing is competitive and needs no membership gymnastics beyond opening the account:

  • Fixed Rate Cash ISAs: 5-year 4.70%, 3-year 4.65%, 2-year 4.55%, 1-year 4.50% — sole accounts only, 18+
  • Fixed Rate Online Bonds: 5-year 4.65%, 3-year 4.60%, 2-year 4.55%, 1-year 4.50% — available from age 16

Early access to a fixed cash ISA closes the account and incurs a charge, so treat the term as binding. Against the field, the 4.70% five-year ISA is now well behind Aldermore's 5.03% three-year and Close Brothers' 5.12% five-year ISA. Note the shape of Nationwide's own curve: the one and two-year rungs have risen to 4.50% and 4.55% while the three and five-year have not moved, so there is only 20 basis points of reward for committing four extra years — but Nationwide is the only one of the three you can also walk into a branch to discuss, and the only one that will open a fixed bond for a 16-year-old.

Age range is a genuine strength: Nationwide serves savers from 11 upwards, where three of the four rivals here start at 18.

sections.heading: £100 Fairer Share and the mutual dividend
sections.html:
In June 2026 Nationwide paid £100 to around 4.4 million members — roughly £440m distributed, the fourth year running. Qualification requires using Nationwide for everyday banking and holding a qualifying savings or mortgage product; the criteria are set each year, so eligibility is not automatic.

Priced into a savings decision, £100 is material on a small balance and negligible on a large one. On £2,400 of regular saver deposits it dwarfs the interest; on £100,000 it is worth 0.10%, which will not bridge the gap between an Instant Access Saver at 1.10% and Close Brothers at 3.85%. No shareholder-owned provider in this comparison pays anything equivalent.

sections.heading: The Virgin Money overlap and the 1.10% problem
sections.html:
Two things could cost you money here.

First, FSCS cover is shared with Virgin Money. Nationwide states plainly that money across all your Nationwide and Virgin Money accounts is covered up to £120,000 per eligible person, or a combined £240,000 for joint accounts. Anyone consolidating savings across both brands on the assumption of separate cover is exposed.

Second, the open-access rates. The Instant Access Saver at 1.10–1.20% tiered and Flex Instant Saver at 2.30% are the weakest unconditional rates in this cluster, against Close Brothers' unconditional 3.85%. If your money needs to be reachable without withdrawal counting, Nationwide is expensive.

On external validation, Nationwide is not a Which? Recommended Provider for savings and is absent from the Defaqto Banking Award 2026 recipient list. The Financial Ombudsman Service recorded 3,001 new cases between 1 July 2025 and 31 March 2026, the second-highest here — though on a far larger member base than Cynergy, Aldermore or Close Brothers. Uphold percentages are unverified. Note too that the Flex Regular Saver and Flex Instant Saver are online only, despite the branch network.

pros: Explicit pledge never to run new-customer-only savings accounts or teaser bonuses
Flex Regular Saver at 6.50% AER on £200 a month for current account holders
FlexOne Saver at 5.00% on up to £5,000 for 11–17 year olds — unmatched in this comparison
£100 Fairer Share Payment made to around 4.4 million members in June 2026, the fourth consecutive year
Fixed Rate Cash ISAs to 4.70% and online bonds to 4.65%, with bonds available from age 16
Member-owned mutual with a branch network, serving savers from age 11 upwards
cons: Instant Access Saver at 1.10–1.20% and Flex Instant Saver at 2.30% are the worst open-access rates in this set
Exceeding the withdrawal allowance drops the Flex Regular Saver and Triple Access accounts to 1.05%
Best rates are gated behind membership and a Nationwide current account
FSCS cover is shared with Virgin Money — a combined £120,000, not £120,000 per brand
Flex Regular Saver and Flex Instant Saver are online only

Not a Which? Recommended Provider for savings and absent from the Defaqto Banking Award 2026 list
3,001 new FOS cases between July 2025 and March 2026
verdict: Nationwide is built for the member, not the shopper. If you hold a Nationwide current account, can feed the 6.50% Flex Regular Saver at £200 a month and qualify for the £100 Fairer Share, the total package beats what the headline rates alone suggest — and you never have to re-shop to avoid a bonus expiring. Families with an 11–17 year old have a further reason to be here: 5.00% on a teenager's balance is not available from any of the other four. It is a bad home for a lump sum you might need to touch. At 1.10–1.20% instant access, with a 1.05% penalty rate waiting behind every withdrawal allowance and FSCS cover shared with Virgin Money, savers with larger unrestricted balances should be looking at Close Brothers instead.

faqs.q: Does Nationwide really never offer bonus rates to new customers?
faqs.a: That is its stated policy: the top savings accounts are for existing members and it says it will not offer new-customer-only savings accounts. The practical effect is a lower entry rate than bonus-led rivals but no scheduled drop after twelve months.

faqs.q: What happens if I make too many withdrawals?
faqs.a: The penalty is severe. Exceed three withdrawals on the Flex Regular Saver, or three on a 1 Year Triple Access Saver or ISA, and the rate falls to 1.05% — losing the great majority of your interest. The Children's Future Saver drops to 1.35% after two withdrawals.

faqs.q: Am I covered twice if I save with both Nationwide and Virgin Money?
faqs.a: No. Nationwide states that money across all your Nationwide and Virgin Money accounts is covered to a combined £120,000 per eligible person, or £240,000 for joint accounts. Spread larger balances across genuinely separate licences.

faqs.q: Will I get the £100 Fairer Share Payment if I only save with Nationwide?
faqs.a: Unlikely on its own. Qualification requires using Nationwide for everyday banking as well as holding a qualifying savings or mortgage product, and the criteria are set afresh each year. Around 4.4 million members qualified for the June 2026 payment.

faqs.q: Can a child or teenager save with Nationwide?
faqs.a: Yes, and this is a real strength. The FlexOne Saver pays 5.00% on up to £5,000 for 11–17 year olds holding a FlexOne account, and the Children's Future Saver pays 2.80% on up to £5,000 a year. Fixed rate online bonds open from age 16.

title: Close Brothers Savings: £10,000 Minimum, 4.85% Ceiling
meta_description: Every Close Brothers account starts at £10,000. In return: 3.85% easy access with no bonus, bonds to 5.34% and two Moneyfacts 2026 provider awards.
intro:
Every Close Brothers savings product starts at £10,000. There is no £1 taster account, no £25 regular saver, nothing for a child. Cynergy and Santander open at £1 and Aldermore from £25 — Close Brothers has drawn its line an order of magnitude higher, and that single rule defines the brand as a consolidation home for larger balances rather than a place to start saving.

What you get for clearing the bar is pricing without gimmicks. The Easy Access account pays 3.85% AER variable with unlimited withdrawals and no bonus attached. Cynergy's 4.15% only beats it because 2.00 percentage points of that number expire after twelve months, leaving a published 2.15% underneath, and Cynergy has closed that account to new customers anyway. At the fixed end, the five-year bond pays 5.34% AER, the three-year 5.18% and the two-year 5.16% — the best fixed rates in this comparison.

The complication is upstream. Close Brothers Group has been provisioning heavily for motor finance redress, raising its provision to £300m from £165m ahead of the FCA scheme, with further provisions since. Deposits stay FSCS-protected, but no other provider here carries an active, quantified conduct liability of that scale.

sections.heading: The £10,000 floor
sections.html:
Minimum £10,000, maximum £2,000,000 — on every product, easy access and fixed alike. There is no starter tier below it. The variable accounts do now publish a sub-£10,000 rate rather than simply refusing the balance, but it is 1.00% AER: if your easy access balance slips under the floor, the rate falls from 3.85% to 1.00%, which is a penalty rather than a tier.

That rules Close Brothers out for most first-time savers and for anyone building a pot from monthly income; there is no regular saver, and no products for under-18s. It also means you cannot split a modest sum across two Close Brothers accounts to blend liquidity and rate — £20,000 buys you exactly two products, and only if you commit £10,000 to each.

For a saver with £50,000 or £150,000, the calculation inverts. A high floor is no obstacle, the rates are consistently near the top of the market, and dealing with one provider across easy access, notice and fixed reduces the admin. Bear in mind the FSCS limit of £120,000 per eligible person (£240,000 joint) sits well below the £2,000,000 account maximum — anything above the limit is unprotected, so genuinely large balances still need splitting across licences. Close Brothers Savings does not share its licence with another retail savings brand.

sections.heading: 3.85% easy access with nothing hidden in it
sections.html:
The Easy Access account pays 3.85% AER variable with unlimited withdrawals. There is no bonus period, no withdrawal counter, no monthly funding requirement and no linked current account.

Set that against the alternatives in this cluster. Cynergy's 4.15% is 2.00 points of bonus over a published underlying rate of 2.15%, and is closed to new customers. Santander's Easy Access Saver is 2.00%. Nationwide's Instant Access Saver is 1.10–1.20%. Aldermore's Easy Access is 2.25%. Judged on what the rate will still be in fourteen months, and with no withdrawal counter attached, 3.85% is the strongest unconditional easy access offer here — provided the balance stays above £10,000.

The 95 Day Notice account pays 4.10% AER variable (again 1.00% below £10,000) and accepts top-ups at any time — a sensible middle rung for money you can plan a quarter ahead for, and one of the few Close Brothers products that will take additional deposits after opening.

sections.heading: Bonds to 5.34%, and a ten-day window to fund them
sections.html:
Fixed Rate Bonds:

  • 5 years — 5.34% AER
  • 3 years — 5.18% AER
  • 2 years — 5.16% AER

The one-year bond has gone: bond terms are now two, three and five years only, so the shortest fixed commitment Close Brothers will take is two years. Fixed Rate Cash ISAs still run over one, two, three and five years and pay 5.12% at five years, 5.11% at three and 5.05% at two. The one-year ISA is the one figure we will not print: Close Brothers’ own ISA hub table says 4.91% and its own one-year product page says 4.84%, and until the two agree there is no single published rate to quote.

The funding mechanics are more forgiving than Cynergy's in one respect and stricter in another. You have a 10-day window to fund a bond or ISA after opening (Cynergy allows 14), but the money can arrive in multiple transfers rather than a single payment — useful if you are drawing funds from several places or working around bank transfer limits. Once the window closes, bonds accept no further deposits and no withdrawals at all until maturity.

Two ISA restrictions deserve attention. Early exit from a fixed cash ISA costs 90 days' interest at one year, 150 at two, 270 at three and 365 at five, and a Fixed Rate Cash ISA cannot be topped up in subsequent tax years — each year's allowance needs a fresh account.

sections.heading: Interest paid away, not rolled up
sections.html:
Close Brothers pays fixed bond interest annually and/or at maturity to a nominated account, and does not compound it. That is a genuine split in the market and it cuts both ways. Note the limit of the rule: the easy access, notice and cash ISA accounts all pay interest into the account itself and do compound it, so this applies to the bonds and nothing else.

For someone living off their savings — a retiree drawing income, or anyone wanting the interest out of the account and into spending money — this is exactly right, and it is something Cynergy cannot do at all, since its bond interest is paid into the bond and cannot be paid away.

For an accumulator, uncompounded interest is a real cost over a five-year term. If you intend to reinvest, you have to do it manually each year and at whatever rate is available then, rather than earning the contracted rate on the growing balance. Factor that in before comparing a Close Brothers five-year bond with a compounding alternative.

sections.heading: The motor finance question at group level
sections.html:
This is the standout negative and it belongs in any honest assessment. Close Brothers Group raised its motor finance redress provision to £300m from £165m ahead of the FCA's redress scheme, covering discretionary commission arrangements dating back to 2007, and has taken further provisions since as disclosed in its half-year results.

What this does not mean: your deposits are unprotected. Savings remain covered by the FSCS up to £120,000 per eligible person. What it does mean is that, alone among the five providers here, Close Brothers carries an active and quantified conduct-redress liability at group level, and savers who prefer not to hold money with a business in that position have a legitimate reason to look elsewhere.

The complaint numbers reflect the same issue rather than the savings business. The Financial Ombudsman Service recorded 671 new cases against Close Brothers Limited between 1 July 2025 and 31 March 2026 — around nine times Aldermore's volume and eight times Cynergy's — though the great majority relate to motor finance rather than to savings accounts. Uphold percentages are unverified.

On recognition, Close Brothers won two categories at the Moneyfacts Compare Awards 2026 on 9 February 2026: Fixed Rate Savings Provider of the Year and ISA Provider of the Year — the only provider-level Moneyfacts wins in this group. It is not a Which? Recommended Provider and does not appear on the Defaqto Banking Award 2026 list.

Best fixed rates in this comparison: 5.34% over five years, 5.18% over three and 5.16% over two

Moneyfacts Compare Awards 2026 winner in two categories — Fixed Rate Savings Provider and ISA Provider of the Year

cons: £10,000 minimum on every single product — the highest entry barrier of the five providers here, and variable accounts drop to 1.00% below it
Close Brothers Group's motor finance redress provision was raised to £300m from £165m, with further provisions since — the only active quantified conduct liability in this set
671 new FOS cases from July 2025 to March 2026, mostly motor finance rather than savings

verdict: Close Brothers is a deposit-consolidation proposition for someone with £10,000 or more per account and no need for a starter product, a regular saver or anything for a child. It suits an income saver particularly well — interest paid away to a nominated account is something Cynergy structurally cannot offer — and it suits anyone who wants an easy access rate that will not quietly halve on its first birthday, so long as the balance stays above £10,000. Two Moneyfacts provider awards in 2026 back up the pricing. Two groups should look elsewhere: savers building a pot from monthly income, who cannot clear the £10,000 floor and should use Aldermore or Cynergy; and anyone uncomfortable holding money with a group carrying an active motor finance redress liability, however well protected the deposits themselves are.

faqs.q: Is £10,000 really the minimum on every account?
faqs.a: Yes. Every Close Brothers savings product, easy access and fixed alike, requires £10,000 to open, with a £2,000,000 maximum. There is no lower tier. Savers with smaller sums should look at Aldermore, which starts at £25 on its Regular Saver and £100 on Easy Access, or Cynergy, which opens from £1.

faqs.q: Should the motor finance provisions worry a saver?
faqs.a: Your deposits remain covered by the FSCS up to £120,000 per eligible person, so the protection is unaffected. The point is one of preference and reputation: Close Brothers Group raised its motor finance redress provision to £300m from £165m ahead of the FCA scheme and has provisioned further since, making it the only provider in this comparison with an active, quantified conduct liability. Keep balances within the FSCS limit and judge the rest on your own comfort.

faqs.q: Why does Close Brothers' 3.85% beat Cynergy's 4.15%?
faqs.a: On the headline it does not — on the underlying rate it does. Cynergy's 4.15% includes a 2.00 percentage point bonus that expires after twelve months, leaving a published 2.15%. Close Brothers pays 3.85% with no bonus and no withdrawal limit, so the comparison flips in year two. In practice the question is academic for a new saver: Cynergy has closed that account to new customers.

faqs.q: Can I have my interest paid into my current account?
faqs.a: Yes. Close Brothers pays interest away annually and/or at maturity to a nominated account and does not compound it. That works well for income savers. If you want the interest to roll up and earn at the contracted rate, this is a drawback over a five-year term — you would need to reinvest manually each year.

faqs.q: Can I add to a Close Brothers bond or cash ISA later?
faqs.a: Bonds and fixed ISAs accept deposits only during the 10-day funding window after opening, though the money can arrive in several transfers. After that, no top-ups and no withdrawals until maturity. Fixed Rate Cash ISAs also cannot be topped up in subsequent tax years, so each year's allowance needs a new account. The 95 Day Notice account is the exception and accepts top-ups at any time.
